subject: english-language
title: Email, Meetings and Memos
welcome_lead: Modern workplaces run on text. Examine email register, meeting talk and the genre of the memo.
meta_desc: Workplace email, meetings and memos as written occupational discourse at A-Level.
final_note: You have audited the prose of contemporary work — clipped, polite and laden with FTAs.

concepts.def: Hybrid of speech and writing; openings, sign-offs and politeness vary by status and familiarity.
Genre with chairs allocating turns, agendas constraining topic and minutes formalising outcomes.
Brief written directive with To/From/Subject headers and clear action points.
Softening of FTAs with hedges, conditionals and politeness markers ('Could I ask...').
Brand-consistent register imposed by style guides — friendly but authoritative.
Workplace communication combines text, images, links and emoji — meaning across modes.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Email salutations index status. Dear Professor X signals formality; Hi Sarah signals familiarity; Hey! can mark in-group casualness.

Sign-offs follow the same gradient, from Yours sincerely to Cheers.

In meetings the chair allocates turns, restricts topic to the agenda and summarises outcomes. Powerful contributors deploy declaratives; less powerful ones use hedged proposals.

Minutes turn talk into action, transforming spoken commitments into written record.

Memos compress directive function into a small space: headers, single-topic body, action points. Modal verbs (will, should, must) project authority.

The genre has migrated to internal email threads but the conventions persist.
